---
title: "A horizontal line that settles a misprint"
subtitle: "Reproducing Denuit (2019), Section 6.1"
---

## Context and problem

@Denuit2019 connects the conditional mean risk sharing rule to the **size-biased transform**. The rule allocates $\kappa_i(s) = \mathsf E[X_i \mid S = s]$ to participant $i$; the paper's representation formula rewrites that conditional expectation in terms of the size-biased version $\widetilde{X}_i$, whose density is $x f_i(x)/\mathsf E[X_i]$, and then reads off closed forms for compound Poisson and compound negative binomial pools.

The practical payoff is a result the paper uses in its own example and which is worth stating on its own: if two participants have the **same claim severity distribution**, then their combined share of any total loss $s$ is the ratio of their combined expected claim frequency to the pool's, *independent of $s$*. Pooling participants with a common severity collapses to pooling frequencies.

That statement is an exact invariant, which makes this a reproduction with something firmer than a figure to check against.

## Paper solution and gold standard

Section 6.1 describes a four participant peer to peer pool. Severities take values in $\{1,2,3,4\}$, frequencies are Poisson, and case 1 sets $\lambda = (0.08, 0.08, 0.10, 0.10)$.

The paper publishes three things this page can check:

1. the shares at $s = 1$: participant 1 contributes 0.178, participant 2 contributes 0.267, participant 3 contributes 0.222, participant 4 contributes 0.333,
2. that the 99.9% quantile of $S$ is 11 in case 1,
3. that Figure 1 shows "an horizontal line ... separating the shares of participants 1-2 from the share of participants 3-4", because participants 1 and 3 share a severity distribution and so do 2 and 4, so 1 and 2 together always contribute $(\lambda_1 + \lambda_2)/\lambda_\bullet$.

### A discrepancy that has to be resolved first

The paper's table and the paper's text disagree about participant 3. The text says plainly that "Participants 1 and 3 have identical severity distributions, as well as participants 2 and 4", which makes participant 3's severity $(0.1, 0.2, 0.4, 0.3)$, the same as participant 1's. The table column for participant 3, as I read it, prints $(0.1, 0.2, 0.3, 0.4)$, with the last two entries swapped.

Only one of those can produce the horizontal line, so the paper's own Figure 1 decides it.

```{python}
#| label: setup
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from aggregate import build
from aggregate.constants import FIG_W, FIG_H
from greater_tables import GT

LAM = [0.08, 0.08, 0.10, 0.10]
SEV_A = '[.1 .2 .4 .3]'        # participant 1, and participant 3 per the text
SEV_B = '[.15 .25 .3 .3]'      # participants 2 and 4
SEV_TABLE3 = '[.1 .2 .3 .4]'   # participant 3 as the table column reads
PAPER_S1 = [0.178, 0.267, 0.222, 0.333]

def pool(sev3, name='Denuit61'):
    return build(f'''port {name}
    agg P1 {LAM[0]} claims dsev [1 2 3 4] {SEV_A} poisson
    agg P2 {LAM[1]} claims dsev [1 2 3 4] {SEV_B} poisson
    agg P3 {LAM[2]} claims dsev [1 2 3 4] {sev3} poisson
    agg P4 {LAM[3]} claims dsev [1 2 3 4] {SEV_B} poisson
''', bs=1, log2=10)

rows = []
for label, sev3, nm in [('text: participant 3 matches participant 1', SEV_A, 'D61a'),
                        ('table column 3 as printed', SEV_TABLE3, 'D61b')]:
    p = pool(sev3, nm)
    d = p.density_df
    share12 = np.array([float(d.loc[s, 'exeqa_P1'] + d.loc[s, 'exeqa_P2']) / s
                        for s in range(1, 16)])
    rows.append({'reading': label,
                 'participants 1+2 share, min over s = 1..15': share12.min(),
                 'max': share12.max(),
                 'constant to 1e-9': bool(np.ptp(share12) < 1e-9)})
GT(pd.DataFrame(rows).set_index('reading'), float_format=6)
```

The text's reading gives a share for participants 1 and 2 that is constant to machine precision over the whole plotted range. The table's reading wanders between 0.41 and 0.48 and has no horizontal line anywhere. Figure 1 shows a horizontal line, so the text is right and the table's third column is wrong, and the rest of this page uses the text.

Whether the fault is in the published table or in my scan of it I cannot tell, so this is recorded as a discrepancy rather than as an erratum.

## The `aggregate` reproduction

Each participant is one `agg` with a Poisson frequency and a four point discrete severity. $\kappa_i$ is the `exeqa_` column, so no allocation code is needed.

```{python}
#| label: program
p = pool(SEV_A)
print(p.program)
```

```{python}
#| label: invariants
d = p.density_df
GT(pd.DataFrame([
    {'quantity': 'E[S] from the pool', 'value': p.est_m,
     'exact': sum(l * m for l, m in zip(LAM, [
         (np.array([1, 2, 3, 4]) * np.array([.1, .2, .4, .3])).sum(),
         (np.array([1, 2, 3, 4]) * np.array([.15, .25, .3, .3])).sum(),
         (np.array([1, 2, 3, 4]) * np.array([.1, .2, .4, .3])).sum(),
         (np.array([1, 2, 3, 4]) * np.array([.15, .25, .3, .3])).sum()]))},
    {'quantity': '99.9% quantile of S', 'value': p.q(0.999), 'exact': 11},
    {'quantity': '(lam1 + lam2) / lam total',
     'value': sum(LAM[:2]) / sum(LAM), 'exact': 0.16 / 0.36},
]).set_index('quantity'), float_format=6)
```

```{python}
#| label: shares-at-1
got = [float(d.loc[1, f'exeqa_P{i}']) for i in (1, 2, 3, 4)]
GT(pd.DataFrame({'participant': [1, 2, 3, 4], 'aggregate share at s = 1': got,
                 'paper': PAPER_S1,
                 'difference': [g - q for g, q in zip(got, PAPER_S1)]}
                ).set_index('participant'),
   formatters={'aggregate share at s = 1': 6, 'paper': 3,
               'difference': '{x:+.5f}'})
```

All four published shares reproduce to within 0.0003, which is the paper's rounding to three decimals: 0.17778 against 0.178, 0.26667 against 0.267, 0.22222 against 0.222, 0.33333 against 0.333. The 99.9% quantile is 11 as stated.

The paper derives those four numbers by hand, from the observation that $S = 1$ implies exactly one claim of size 1, so the shares are the relative probabilities of that claim belonging to each participant. That gives $\lambda_i \Pr[C_i = 1]$ normalized, which is a check that needs no software at all.

```{python}
#| label: by-hand
w = np.array([LAM[0] * 0.1, LAM[1] * 0.15, LAM[2] * 0.1, LAM[3] * 0.15])
GT(pd.DataFrame({'participant': [1, 2, 3, 4],
                 'lam_i P[C_i = 1], normalized': w / w.sum(),
                 'aggregate': got, 'paper': PAPER_S1}).set_index('participant'),
   float_format=6)
```

The three agree, so the closed form, the library and the paper all say the same thing at $s = 1$.

### Figure 1

```{python}
#| label: figure-1
#| fig-cap: "Reproducing Figure 1. Share of the total loss contributed by each participant, and the horizontal separation at 4/9."
ss = np.arange(1, 16)
sh = pd.DataFrame(
    {f'participant {i}': [float(d.loc[s, f'exeqa_P{i}']) / s for s in ss]
     for i in (1, 2, 3, 4)}, index=ss)
fig, axs = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(2 * FIG_W, FIG_H), layout='constrained')
sh.plot(ax=axs[0], lw=1, marker='.', ms=3)
axs[0].set(xlabel='s', ylabel='share of s', title='individual shares', ylim=(0, 0.5))
axs[0].legend(fontsize=6)
(sh['participant 1'] + sh['participant 2']).plot(
    ax=axs[1], lw=1, marker='.', ms=3, label='participants 1 + 2')
(sh['participant 3'] + sh['participant 4']).plot(
    ax=axs[1], lw=1, marker='.', ms=3, label='participants 3 + 4')
for y in (sum(LAM[:2]) / sum(LAM), sum(LAM[2:]) / sum(LAM)):
    axs[1].axhline(y, ls='--', lw=0.6, c='C7')
axs[1].set(xlabel='s', ylabel='share of s', title='the horizontal separation',
           ylim=(0, 1))
axs[1].legend(fontsize=6)
```

The left panel is the paper's figure: four irregular curves, the irregularity coming from the discreteness of the severities, with participant 1 below participant 2 throughout because its severity is the lighter of the two. The right panel is the invariant, and the two group shares sit exactly on $4/9$ and $5/9$ at every $s$ while the individual shares inside them move.

## Comments

### The invariant is the reproduction

The four numbers at $s = 1$ are a good check and a weak one: they are determined by a single event, one claim of size one, and the paper computes them by hand precisely because that case is elementary. Any implementation that got the frequencies and the first severity probability right would match them.

The horizontal line is the strong check, and it is strong for a structural reason. It holds at every $s$ simultaneously, it depends on the whole severity distribution rather than one point of it, and it comes out of the paper's representation formula rather than out of arithmetic. Getting it to machine precision at fifteen values of $s$ says the conditional expectation kernel is right, not merely that the inputs were typed correctly.

It is also the check that resolved the table discrepancy, which is the useful thing about invariants: a wrong input that still satisfies the published point values can be caught by a structure the published point values do not see.

### What the pool is, and what it is not

There is a compound distribution here, unlike the two @Denuit2025a and @Denuit2025 chapters, where each agent carried one certain claim. Each participant has a Poisson claim count, so the frequency machinery is exercised, and the severities are genuinely discrete so no discretization error enters anywhere: `bs = 1` is exact on a severity supported on $\{1,2,3,4\}$.

That makes this the cleanest of the three risk sharing reproductions numerically, and the least interesting economically. The frequencies are small, 0.08 to 0.10, so the pool's total is zero most of the time and the whole allocation question concerns the conditional distribution given that something happened. A real pool has enough participants for the law of large numbers to matter, which is what @Denuit2022b takes up.
